feat: Generate M3U playlist files for Spotify playlists

Adds an EXTM3U export so playlists are visible as a single unit in
Jellyfin (and any media server that scans M3U) instead of a pile of
loose tracks. When a playlist URL is pasted, a "Generate M3U playlist
file" checkbox appears next to the input (default on); after every
track has been processed, Downtify writes the playlist to
``<downloads>/Playlists/<sanitized-name>.m3u`` with relative track
paths (so the same file works across mounts — Downtify's
``/downloads`` and Jellyfin's ``/nas/music`` resolve identically).
Failed or unmatched tracks are skipped and logged.

Backend
- ``downtify/m3u.py`` (new): ``sanitize_playlist_name``,
  ``build_m3u_content``, ``write_m3u``. Stdlib only. Track lines are
  computed via ``os.path.relpath(track, start=m3u_dir)``.
- ``downtify/api.py``: new ``POST /api/playlist/m3u`` endpoint that
  accepts ``{playlist_url, tracks}`` and resolves the playlist name
  server-side via the existing ``playlist_info_and_tracks`` helper —
  no changes to ``GET /api/song/url`` shape.

Frontend
- Checkbox in ``SearchInput.vue``, visible only when the URL parses
  as a playlist.
- ``download.js`` waits on all per-track downloads, then posts the
  M3U with successful tracks in original order.

Tests / CI
- ``tests/test_m3u.py`` — 19 unit tests covering sanitisation,
  ordering, missing-file skipping, EXTINF formatting, UTF-8/no-BOM/LF
  encoding, and relative-path resolution for both flat and nested
  layouts.
- ``pytest`` added as dev dep; new ``uv run pytest`` step in
  ``test.yml`` next to ruff.

Docs
- README: new "M3U playlist export" section.

feat: Move M3U toggle to Settings + auto-regen for Playlist Monitor

Replaces the per-paste "Generate M3U" checkbox with a single global
setting under Settings → Playlists, default on, that governs both
manual playlist downloads AND Playlist Monitor sweeps. Monitored
playlists now get an up-to-date ``Playlists/<name>.m3u`` after every
sweep that downloads at least one new track — instead of a stale
file from initial paste-down (or no file at all for Monitor-only
playlists).

Backend
- ``api.py``: new ``generate_m3u: True`` in DEFAULT_SETTINGS, accepted
  by the existing ``/api/settings/update`` endpoint. The initial
  ``check_playlist`` call from ``add_monitor_playlist`` now passes
  ``state.settings`` through.
- ``downloader.py``: new ``Downloader.existing_filename_for(song)``
  that mirrors ``download()``'s post-conversion path resolution —
  prefers ``{basename}.{audio_format}`` and falls back to any
  ``{basename}.*``. Returns ``None`` when nothing matches.
- ``monitor.py``: ``check_playlist`` and ``monitor_loop`` accept an
  optional ``settings`` dict. After a sweep that downloads at least
  one new track, ``_regenerate_m3u`` walks the full ordered playlist,
  resolves each track via the downloader, and rewrites the M3U with
  whatever survives the existence check.
- ``main.py``: passes ``api.state.settings`` into ``monitor_loop``.

Frontend
- New "Playlists" section in ``Settings.vue`` with a checkbox bound
  to ``settings.generate_m3u``.
- ``download.js`` reads the setting (defaults to true) instead of an
  options arg; manual paste-down behaviour is preserved.

Docs
- README updated to describe the unified toggle and the Monitor
  integration path.

fix: save MP3 tags as ID3v2.4 instead of v2.3

ID3v2.3 has no UTF-8 text encoding (only Latin-1/UTF-16), so saving
v2.3 frames created with encoding=3 (used throughout _tag_mp3 and
embed_lyrics) forces mutagen to transcode them to UTF-16 on write.

On a self-hosted instance running mutagen 1.47.0, this was observed
to corrupt the written title tag (garbage characters appended, real
characters dropped from the tail), which desynced the ID3 reader for
every frame written after TIT2 — silently losing artist, album,
genre, date, track number and cover art on read across ~1700
downloaded tracks. Re-tagging the same files with v2_version=4 (no
forced transcode) restored every frame correctly.

I could not isolate a minimal reproduction of the exact trigger in a
synthetic test despite trying several realistic variations (small and
full-size files, pre-existing ffmpeg-written tags, repeated re-saves,
re-tagging one of the actually affected files) — mutagen 1.47.0 did
not corrupt any of them under v2.3 in isolation either. It's possible
the trigger depends on conditions specific to that instance (e.g. the
audio stream itself, given YouTube's SABR rollout was also causing
malformed downloads around the same time) that I couldn't reproduce
here. ID3v2.4 supports UTF-8 natively, so switching to it removes the
forced-transcode code path regardless of what exactly triggers it.

Added round-trip tests for both save paths (_tag_mp3, embed_lyrics)
to guard the v2.4 behavior going forward.

fix: enable yt-dlp's remote EJS component for YouTube SABR fallback

YouTube's SABR-only streaming experiment is gating audio formats for
the `ios`/`android` player clients (yt-dlp #12482). The only real
fallback left is `web`/`web_embedded`, but those need a JS runtime to
solve YouTube's signature/n-challenges — and yt-dlp refuses to fetch
its EJS challenge-solver script unless `--remote-components ejs:*` is
explicitly allowed, even when a JS runtime is installed and detected.

Without this, every player client in the fallback chain effectively
fails once SABR gates ios/android, and downloads either fail outright
or (observed on a self-hosted instance) produce audio with an
audible ~1s gap, presumably from a partial/mismatched stream one of
the later clients did manage to serve. Matches the report and fix in
#247.

- downtify/downloader.py: add `'remote_components': ['ejs:github']`
  to `ydl_opts`.
- Dockerfile: install `deno` (JS runtime, native Alpine/musl build —
  avoids glibc compatibility issues with Deno's official binaries)
  and `yt-dlp-ejs-rt-deno` (the Deno-based EJS challenge solver
  yt-dlp uses), both available in Alpine's community repo.

Verified end-to-end on the self-hosted instance: before this change,
a 100s log window showed repeated download failures
(`FileNotFoundError` / `Unable to rename file`) alongside the SABR
warnings; after installing deno/yt-dlp-ejs-rt-deno and enabling
remote_components, the same window had zero failures.

or missing entirely, on a first run — for however long that one track
took, even though the rest of the playlist was already on disk and
playable.

so the playlist file grows as the download progresses:

- `api._process_batch` — manual playlist/album downloads and CSV
  library imports. Downloads here run concurrently, so each completion
  rewrites the file under a lock to keep writes from interleaving.

`_regenerate_m3u` takes an optional `{track_id: filename}` map. The
per-track rewrites pass it (seeded with the files earlier sweeps left
on disk, then topped up as each track lands) so a rewrite is a cheap
in-memory pass; without it the function resolves every track against
the filesystem as before, which is what the final rewrite still does.
That matters because `existing_filename_for` falls back to globbing
the target directory for tracks with no file yet — doing that for
every track on every write would be quadratic over a large sweep.

A song that was already on disk was downloaded again every time it showed

New `overwrite_existing_files` setting (default `true`, so existing
behavior doesn't change). When it's off, `Downloader.download()` looks
for the song before fetching anything and returns the existing file's
path if it finds one.

- Library-wide lookup (`Downloader.find_existing_download`). The exact
  destination is checked first. After that, the whole download folder is
  scanned for an audio file with the name the output template renders
  for the song, compared case-insensitively. So a playlist download finds
  the song in the library root, in another playlist's folder, or in an
  artist/album folder from a different organize-by setting. If the
  template has folders (e.g. `{artists}/{title}`), they must match too,
  so another artist's song with the same title isn't picked up.

  A first version of this change checked only the exact destination
  path. Playlist tracks are written to a per-playlist folder
  (`_process_batch` / `check_playlist` pass `subdir=<playlist>`), so
  that version never saw copies in the root or in other playlists, and
  those songs were still downloaded again. This commit fixes that.

- Check before the search. For Spotify tracks, which already carry the
  title, artists and album, the check runs before the YouTube Music
  search. Skipping a song then costs no network requests at all.
  `_can_resolve_path_early` turns this off when the template needs a
  field only enrichment can fill in (`{album}` without an album name,
  `{tracknumber}` without a track number). In that case the check waits
  until after enrichment, so an incomplete path can't match an unrelated
  file.

- Duplicates running at the same time. The check and the download run
  under a per-target lock. When the same song is queued twice at once
  (listed twice in one playlist, or in two playlists downloading in
  parallel), the second run waits for the first and then skips instead
  of downloading it again.

  extension is `.mp3`, `.flac`, `.m4a`, `.ogg` or `.opus`. Before, the
  `existing_filename_for` fallback used `glob('{basename}.*')`, which
  could return a leftover `.lrc` sidecar as the track, and which found
  nothing for titles like "Song [Live]" because `[...]` is a glob
  character class. It now lists the directory and compares names
  directly. The M3U regeneration and Player code that call it get the

returns the existing path relative to the download folder. The playlist

fix(match): accept Spotify "- Ao Vivo" titles, fall back to standard YouTube

Users reported downloads failing with "Could not find a YouTube match
for '<song>'" for songs that exist on standard YouTube but not on
YouTube Music, and songs downloading as the wrong recording (e.g. a
Spanish version, the only one on YouTube Music, instead of the English
original available on YouTube). The matcher only ever searched YouTube
Music, with no fallback.

Testing that against a real 19-track live sertanejo playlist showed the
bigger cause: only 2 tracks downloaded. YouTube Music had every track
(same artists, 1s off), but the title gate rejected them — Spotify
names a version "Tubarões - Ao Vivo", YouTube Music "Tubarões (Ao
Vivo)" — and the fallback applies the same gate, so it failed too.

Title/artist gates (downtify/providers.py):
- `_names_match` rewrites a trailing " - Suffix" as " (Suffix)" on both
  sides before comparing (`_DASH_VERSION_SUFFIX_RE`), so
  "Ai Cowboy - BeM Interior, Ao Vivo" matches
  "Ai Cowboy (BeM Interior, Ao Vivo)". Live vs studio still stays apart.
  This flips the old `test_titles_match_rejects_differently_formatted_live_tag`
  (which pinned "Wait It Out - Live" ≠ "Wait It Out (Live)" as
  deliberately strict) into
  `test_titles_match_accepts_differently_formatted_live_tag`; its
  live≠studio neighbors are unchanged and still pass.
- "ao vivo", "en vivo", "acústico"/"acustico" added to
  `_VERSION_QUALIFIER_WORDS`, so a plain studio title no longer matches
  a Portuguese/Spanish-tagged live or acoustic take (or vice versa) —
  previously only English "live"/"acoustic" were caught.
- `_artists_overlap` also splits each candidate credit on `,` `&`
  `and` `feat.` … (shared `_ARTIST_CREDIT_SPLIT_RE`, renamed from
  `_YOUTUBE_ARTIST_SPLIT_RE`), keeping the unsplit name too. YouTube
  Music sometimes packs every artist into one entry ("JIRAYAUAI, DOUTH!,
  VITOR BUENO, GUSTTAVO LIMA, ANA CASTELA, and SAM SAM"), which never
  overlapped Spotify's separate artist list.

Standard-YouTube fallback (downtify/providers.py):
- `find_match` now wraps the existing YouTube Music pipeline (renamed,
  unchanged, to `_find_youtube_music_match`) and falls back to a
  standard-YouTube search when YouTube Music returns no acceptable
  match, or only one whose duration is more than 10s off from the
  source track's (`_STRONG_MATCH_MAX_DURATION_DIFF`) — a strong sign of
  a different recording that shares title and artist.
- A YouTube hit replaces a weak YouTube Music hit only when its
  duration is strictly closer; otherwise the YouTube Music match is
  kept, since catalog uploads usually have the cleanest audio. A
  standard-YouTube match is returned with `match=None` (it carries no
  catalog metadata to enrich from); the source song's own metadata is
  used as-is.
- New `_find_match_via_youtube`: searches via yt-dlp's flat `ytsearch`
  (no new dependency; honors `DOWNTIFY_FORCE_IPV4`) and runs results
  through the same `_pick_best` gates as YouTube Music hits — title
  resemblance, artist overlap — plus:
  - karaoke/cover/instrumental/sped-up/8D… variants rejected against
    the raw video title, before "(Official Audio)"-style noise is
    stripped (otherwise "(Instrumental Audio)" would slip through);
  - a hard 30s duration cap (`_YOUTUBE_MAX_DURATION_DIFF`) so long
    music-video cuts, loops and compilations are never taken;
  - live/upcoming streams skipped.
- New `_youtube_entry_to_result`: derives artists from an
  "Artist - Title" upload title (split on `,` `&` `+` `x` `vs` `and`
  `feat.` `ft.`, keeping the unsplit credit too so "Florence and the
  Machine" still matches) plus the channel name with "- Topic" /
  "VEVO" / "Official" stripped. Featured-artist credits ("(feat. X)",
  "[with X]", trailing "ft. X") and curly apostrophes are normalized on
  both sides, since Spotify and YouTube uploads format them differently.
- Other-language version tags (spanish/español, english, portuguese/
  português, french/français, italian, german, japanese, korean,
  chinese) added to `_VERSION_QUALIFIER_WORDS`, so "Song (Spanish
  Version)" no longer passes the title gate for "Song" — on either
  site.
- `song_from_video_id` calls `_find_youtube_music_match` directly: it
  only wants catalog metadata for an already-pinned video, so a
  standard-YouTube search there would only add latency.

- New coverage: fallback when YouTube Music has nothing; weak YouTube

fix(match): title-first YouTube Music retry, looser title/artist gates for real-world uploads

Some songs still failed with "Could not find a YouTube match", for two
kinds of reasons: the right track was ranked too low by the query the
matcher sends, or it was returned but rejected by the title/artist
gates because of how the upload is labelled.

1. Title-first query retry

For some songs YouTube Music ranks the right track low (4th/5th) or
leaves it out for "<artist> <title>", while "<title> <artist>" returns
it as the very first result. YouTube Music's ranking depends on word
order, and the matcher only ever tried one order.

- The search stages of `_find_youtube_music_match` (unfiltered search
  for the "Top result" card → `songs` shelf → `videos` when that's
  empty → gated first-result loop) moved, unchanged, into a new
  `_search_youtube_music_match(query, title, artists, album, duration)`
  helper, so both word orders go through exactly the same stages and
  gates.
- `_find_youtube_music_match` runs the helper with the existing
  artist-first query; only if that finds nothing does it retry with a
  title-first query (`"<title> <all artists>"`), logging when the retry
  is what resolved the track. The album-tracklist fallback still runs
  last, after both orders miss.
- The retry is skipped when the song has no artists (both orders would
  be the same query).
- Cost: a song not found on the first query makes up to 3 more YouTube
  Music requests before the album/YouTube fallbacks; songs found on the
  first query make no extra requests.

2. Gates rejecting the right track (reported failures)

- "Crazy in Love" by Eden Project: YouTube Music credits "The Eden
  Project", Spotify "Eden Project", so the artist gate failed on an
  otherwise exact match (266s vs 265s). `_artists_overlap` now compares
  names through a new `_norm_artist_name` (casefolded, whitespace
  collapsed, leading "The " dropped) on both sides.
- "Kuchizuke Diamond" by WEAVER: the artist's own upload is in the top
  results, titled "くちづけDiamond - Kuchizuke Diamond" (native script,
  then romanization), which the title gate never matched.
- "Smash Hit Theme" by Douglas Holmquist: only exists as a fan upload
  titled "Smash Hit OST - Smash Hit Theme Full Version - Douglas
  Holmquist" (89s vs 88s) on a channel that isn't the artist.

  Fixes:
  - `_titles_match` also accepts a title matching one " - "-separated
    segment of the other title (either direction). Guards: the segment
    must start with the whole title (so "Smash Hit" never matches
    "Smash Hit Theme", and "Storm" never matches "A Perfect Storm"),
    and the remaining segments must not contain a version qualifier
    (so "Yellow" still doesn't match "Yellow - Live" or
    "Coldplay - Yellow - Remix"). Spotify's " - Ao Vivo" suffix is
    normalized on the whole-title side first, so "Tubarões - Ao Vivo"
    matches "Diego & Victor Hugo - Tubarões (Ao Vivo)" but not
    "Diego & Victor Hugo - Tubarões".
  - `_youtube_entry_to_result` (standard-YouTube fallback) credits
    every " - " segment of an upload's title as a possible artist, not
    only the first — "Game OST - Title - Artist" uploads put the artist
    last. Title, artist and version gates plus the 30s duration cap
    still apply, so "How I wrote the Smash Hit Theme music" (315s) and
    the "(Looping)" cut (77s, 11s off) lose to the full version.

All earlier matching fixes are kept as-is: " - Ao Vivo" vs "(Ao Vivo)",
packed artist credits, live/acoustic/other-language qualifiers, and the
standard-YouTube fallback.

Tests (tests/test_providers.py):
- New `_FakeYTMByQuery` fake that routes results by query text and
  records every query sent.
- Title-first retry: resolves a track the artist-first query misses
  (album fallback not reached); not sent after an artist-first hit;
  joins all artists; a song without artists runs one round only; the
  album fallback still runs after both orders miss.
- Title segments: accepted for the three real-world shapes above, in
  both directions; rejected for a shorter segment, a live/remix rest,
  a dash-suffixed live target vs a studio segment, and mere
  containment.
- `_artists_overlap` ignores a leading "The" (and still rejects "EDEN"
  for "Eden Project").
- YouTube fallback credits the artist from the last title segment and
  picks the closest-duration cut; `find_match` picks the artist's own
  romanized-segment upload over a fan lyric video.

Docs:
- docs/how-it-works.md: the audio-match section mentions the
  title-first retry, the leading-"The" artist normalization and the
  title-segment matching.

fix(download): honor the chosen bitrate for M4A/OPUS, fix OGG conversion crash

Reported: with M4A at any bitrate, Downtify produced 128 kbps AAC files.

Root cause: yt-dlp's `FFmpegExtractAudio` stream-copies instead of
encoding whenever the downloaded stream already has the target codec —
an AAC source for M4A (and an Opus source for OPUS) — and then silently
ignores `preferredquality`. Whenever YouTube serves its ~128 kbps AAC
stream (itag 140, or the AAC track of format 18), M4A came out at the
source's bitrate whatever was chosen. Reproduced with the real
postprocessor: the same AAC source became a 128 kbps M4A at "320" but a
320 kbps MP3 at "320". An Opus source for OPUS was likewise copied at
~150 kbps regardless of the setting.

While testing every format through the same code path, OGG turned out to
be broken outright: Downtify passed `preferredcodec='ogg'`, but yt-dlp
names Ogg Vorbis "vorbis", so the conversion crashed with
`KeyError: 'ogg'` (reproduced on the pinned yt-dlp 2026.8.19, the same
version the Docker image installs).

downtify/downloader.py:
- New `_ExtractAudioPP`, a subclass of yt-dlp's `FFmpegExtractAudioPP`,
  replaces the `postprocessors` entry in `ydl_opts` and is registered via
  `ydl.add_post_processor(..., when='post_process')` (`ydl_opts` only
  accepts built-in postprocessors by name). It overrides only
  `get_audio_codec`: when the source codec matches the target (AAC→M4A,
  Opus→OPUS, Vorbis→OGG) it reads the source bitrate with ffprobe and,
  unless it's already within 10% of the chosen bitrate
  (`_BITRATE_COPY_TOLERANCE`), reports the codec under a non-matching
  name. That sends yt-dlp's own `run()` down its normal encode path, so
  encoder choice (incl. libfdk_aac when available), `-b:a` arguments and
  temp-file handling stay yt-dlp's. A source already at the chosen
  bitrate — e.g. YouTube's 128 kbps AAC for M4A @ 128 — is still copied
  losslessly; an unknown bitrate or an ffprobe failure also keeps the
  copy. Re-encodes are logged at INFO.
- New pure `_audio_bit_rate(ffprobe_json)`: the audio stream's
  `bit_rate`, falling back to the container's only for audio-only files
  (WebM/Ogg streams carry no per-stream rate; a video stream would
  inflate the container rate).
- `_YTDLP_AUDIO_CODECS` maps Downtify's `ogg` to yt-dlp's `vorbis`
  (output is still `.ogg`, so file naming/tagging is unchanged).

perf: parallelize downloads, metadata lookups, Spotify paging and library tag reads

A pass over the codebase for work that was running sequentially or
blocking the event loop, fixed with threads/async where it measurably
helps. Nothing here changes an endpoint, setting or response shape.

Event loop (downtify/api.py, downtify/monitor.py)
- `POST /api/download/url` and `POST /api/download/album` are `async`
  endpoints but resolved the Spotify / YouTube Music metadata with a
  plain synchronous call, freezing every other request and WebSocket
  for as long as that network round-trip took. Both now run it via
  `asyncio.to_thread`. Measured on a real track download: the worst
  `/api/health` latency during the request went from 314–374 ms on
  main to 71–78 ms.
- `reconcile_downloaded_tracks` ran one `Path.exists()` per downloaded
  track directly on the event loop — thousands of stats on a slow disk
  or network mount. Moved to a worker thread.
- `ConnectionManager.broadcast` serializes the message once and sends
  to all clients concurrently (`asyncio.gather`) instead of one after
  another, so a slow client no longer delays everyone's progress
  updates. A socket is only dropped if it's still the registered one
  (the client may have reconnected mid-send).

Dedicated download thread pool (downtify/downloader.py)
- Downloads (API single/batch/album and Playlist Monitor sweeps) ran on
  asyncio's default executor: `min(32, cpu_count + 4)` threads, e.g. 6
  on a 2-core NAS. With "Parallel downloads" allowed up to 30, a higher
  setting was silently capped, and every `asyncio.to_thread()` call
  (M3U writes, Monitor DB queries, playlist fetches, cookie upload)
  queued behind downloads that hold a thread for minutes. They now use
  `DOWNLOAD_EXECUTOR`, sized `MAX_PARALLEL_DOWNLOADS + 8` (the extra
  room covers Monitor sweeps, which download outside the semaphore);
  the semaphore still bounds how many actually run.
  `MAX_PARALLEL_DOWNLOADS` moved from api.py to downloader.py so both
  share it; `api.MAX_PARALLEL_DOWNLOADS` is still importable.

Per-download pipeline (downtify/downloader.py)
- The iTunes genre lookup, cover-art download and lyrics fetch depend
  only on the song's metadata, yet ran one after another *after*
  yt-dlp finished. They now start on a small per-download thread pool
  as the download begins, and their results are collected once it's
  done. A failed download doesn't wait for them
  (`shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)`), and a failed lookup
  still never fails the download (logged, treated as "not found").
- The cover was downloaded twice when "Organize by album" is on (once
  for the embedded art, again for `cover.jpg`). It's fetched once and
  passed to both: `embed_metadata(..., cover_bytes=)` and
  `Downloader._save_album_cover(..., cover_bytes)` (both optional, old
  call sites unchanged).
- yt-dlp calls the progress hook for every downloaded chunk, and each
  report became a WebSocket broadcast scheduled on the event loop. It's
  now forwarded only when the whole-number percentage changes (at most
  96 reports per download instead of one per chunk).
- Measured on a real track download: 15.9–16.7 s on main vs
  15.3–15.6 s here.

Spotify playlists (downtify/spotify.py)
- `_graphql_all_tracks` fetched pages strictly one after another. The
  first page reports the playlist size, so the remaining pages are now
  requested concurrently (4 at a time, to stay polite) at fixed
  offsets. If a page other than the last comes back short, fixed
  offsets would skip items, so the rest is walked sequentially from
  that page — the previous behavior. Any page error still propagates to
  the caller, which falls back to the embed data as before.

Library tag reads (main.py, `GET /tracks`)
- The Player and Library pages call `/tracks` on every visit, and it
  re-parsed every file's tags sequentially each time. Tags are now
  cached per file keyed by `(mtime_ns, size)` (entries for removed files
  are pruned on each call), and cache misses are read on 8 threads.
  Benchmark, 2,000 files: a warm request needs only a stat per file
  (0.003 s); a cold read with a simulated 2 ms per-file I/O latency (HDD
  seek / NAS round-trip) drops from 4.95 s sequential to 0.62 s on 8
  threads. On a RAM disk (no I/O latency) threads are ~0.25 s slower
  than sequential for that first read — tag parsing is GIL-bound — which
  was judged worth it since real music libraries sit on disks or NAS
  mounts, and it's a one-time cost per file change.
- Multiprocessing was benchmarked too (4–8 processes: 0.14 s on the RAM
  disk) and rejected: forking a server that has live download threads
  isn't safe, spawning a pool costs more than the parse on typical
  libraries, and the cache removes the repeat cost anyway.

Considered and left alone
- Parallelizing YouTube Music match searches (e.g. the top-result and
  `songs` queries at once) or Playlist Monitor watches: it would multiply
  requests to YouTube and undermine the rate-limit protection the
  delay/parallel-downloads settings exist for.
- The frontend already loads `/tracks` and `/playlists` concurrently
  (`Promise.all`).

Tests
- New tests/test_concurrency.py (17 tests). Where possible they assert
  the concurrency itself with barriers/events, so they hang into a
  timeout (not merely run slower) if the code goes back to sequential:
  the dedicated executor's size and use; both async endpoints resolving
  off the event loop; concurrent broadcast, dropping only failed
  clients, keeping a reconnected one; genre/cover/lyrics lookups
  starting while yt-dlp runs (and the genre reaching the tags); a
  failed download not waiting on a slow lookup; the cover downloaded
  once for tags + cover.jpg; one progress report per whole percent;
  Spotify pages after the first fetched concurrently, a single-page
  playlist making one request, a short middle page falling back to
  sequential; `/tracks` cache hits, invalidation on change, pruning of
  removed files, and tag reads on multiple threads.
- New tests/conftest.py: an autouse fixture stubs the downloader's
  iTunes genre and cover lookups. Because lookups now start before
  yt-dlp runs, tests with a fake YoutubeDL that aborts the download
  would otherwise have fired real HTTP requests in background threads.
  Tests exercising those lookups override it. (Moved there from
  test_downloader_extended.py, where it was first added.)
- Existing fakes of `YoutubeDL` are unchanged apart from that.

feat(podcasts): subscribe to shows, download episodes, remember where you left off

Podcasts are not Spotify tracks routed through YouTube — every episode
is already a finished audio file at an RSS enclosure URL, so this is a
separate, much shorter pipeline: resolve a link to a feed, download the
enclosure, tag it, done. New module `downtify/podcasts.py` plus a
schedule row (see below), everything else in this message is behind it.

Subscribing
- Three ways in: a direct RSS feed URL; a Spotify show or episode link
  (the embed always resolves to the show's latest *episode* — there is
  no separate "show" entity — so the show's name comes from that
  episode's `subtitle`, then gets matched to a feed through the iTunes
  podcast directory; an episode link additionally tries to match its
  own title into the feed); or free-text search, also via iTunes.
- A Spotify-exclusive show (no public feed) is reported as exactly
  that, by name, not silently dropped or guessed at.
- Verified against real, live services before writing a line of the
  parsing code: resolved Radiolab and This American Life by both show
  and episode Spotify links, matched their real iTunes feeds, and
  confirmed a made-up show name correctly returns "no feed" rather than
  a wrong guess.

How many episodes download
- "Every new episode": only the single newest episode downloads on
  first subscribe (not a show's whole back catalog), then whatever is
  new on every check after. Nothing is ever removed automatically.
- "Latest N": a rolling window, enforced on every check including the
  first — older downloaded episodes are pruned to make room. Raising N
  later makes a pruned episode downloadable again.
- An episode removed with "Remove download" is flagged separately
  (`dismissed`) from one a retention prune removed, so a deliberate
  delete is never resurrected by raising N or by a later feed fetch —
  only the automatic kind is reversible.

Scheduling reuses the watcher, not a second one
- `monitor.py` gets a `KIND_PODCAST` watch kind, keyed by feed URL
  instead of a Spotify id; `check_watch` dispatches it to
  `podcasts.sync_show` like it already does for playlists and artists,
  on the same background sweep and the same per-watch interval.
  Podcast-specific state (shows, episodes, retention, playback
  position) lives in its own store, exactly like Liked Songs' playlist
  membership lives beside the generic watch table rather than in it.

Tagging and cover art
- mutagen, same libraries the rest of the app uses, dedicated tagging
  functions (mp3/m4a fully, ogg/opus text-only) rather than editing
  downloader.py's music-only private helpers, which know about
  MusicBrainz release types and album track totals that don't apply
  here. Title, show as album, author as artist, episode/season as
  track/disc number, year, a "Podcast" genre, and the description as a
  comment (stored as plain text — HTML is stripped at parse time, never
  rendered, since sanitizing it for display would be more code for no
  real benefit on a paragraph of show notes).
- Cover art is the larger, by actual pixel size, of the feed's own
  image and iTunes' artwork — same "largest available" idea as music
  covers, just two candidates instead of four.
- Verified live: downloaded a real ~700KB Radiolab episode, confirmed
  title/album/artist/year/genre/comment and a 235KB embedded cover in
  the saved file with mutagen.

  excluded from the music library scan (`library_catalog.py`) so they
  never appear as tracks/albums/artists and an Upgrade library run

  `GET /api/podcasts/shows/{id}/episodes`,

  unlabelled release counts as an album, which is what the albums shelf
  defaults to. At least one kind must stay on. Releases of a kind that's

  all kinds / off.

fix(spotify): write the album tag on single-track downloads

A user reported that every single-track download (a Spotify track link,
or a search result downloaded on its own) came out with no album tag at
all - title, artist, track, date, genre, album artist, lyrics and cover
were fine - so tag-based servers like Navidrome filed it under
"[Unknown Album]". Playlist and album downloads were unaffected.
Long-standing (reported across 2.9.x to 3.1.0).

Cause: a Spotify track is resolved from its embed page
(`track_from_id`), and the *track* embed simply has no album - no
`album` key, no album uri (checked live on the reported track,
3OPpCynaIrfUyBIBYRYIvC). Playlist/album downloads get the album from the
playlist/album embed instead, which is why only single tracks were
affected. The YouTube Music match can fill it in (`enrich_from_match`),
but only when the matched result carries an album, which a music video
or a plain-YouTube fallback often doesn't.

Fix (downtify/spotify.py):
- The public track page (open.spotify.com/track/<id>) names the album in
  its Open Graph tags (`music:album` with the album URL, and
  `music:album:track`). `_album_ref_from_open_track_page` reads those,
  and `_fill_album_from_open_page` then takes the album's name - and its
  track count, plus the track number when the song has none - from the
  album embed, the same source album downloads use. Any failure leaves
  the song as it was: a missing album tag is never worth a failed
  download.
- `track_from_id(track_id, *, with_album=False)`: the lookup costs two
  more requests, so it's opt-in. Callers that already know the album (a
  monitored playlist's row being topped up, the playlist cache, cover
  lookups) are unchanged; the single-track paths turn it on:
  `/api/url` / `/api/url/resolve` / `/api/download/url` for a track link
  (api.py), `spotify.resolve`, and library upgrade's tag refresh when
  the file has no album tag.
- `enrich_track_from_spotify_if_sparse` (which the downloader runs on
  every Spotify song before matching audio) now also enriches a row
  that only lacks the album, with the lookup on. A new
  `with_album=False` keeps an artist's top songs from paying for it -
  their album names come from the artist overview right after.

feat: mobile client support - sign-in, pairing, library sync, streaming, transcoding, LAN discovery

Downtify is getting an official Android app that browses and streams the
library from the user's own server and keeps songs offline, the way
Jellyfin clients do. This adds everything the server side needs, without
changing anything for existing installs: with the new "Require sign-in"
off (the default), every route behaves exactly as before.

Sign-in and pairing (downtify/auth.py, downtify/auth_routes.py)
- Paired devices: Settings > Apps shows a single-use, 5-minute pairing
  code (Crockford base32, `XXXX-XXXX`, ~40 bits) and a QR code carrying
  `downtify://pair?url=&sid=&code=`; `POST /api/auth/pair` trades it for
  a device token `dtfy_<id>_<secret>` (sent as `Authorization: Bearer`).
  Only SHA-256 hashes of tokens, session ids, pairing codes and WS
  tickets are stored; every secret comparison is constant-time. Devices
  are listed (name, platform, last seen, last IP - written at most once a
  minute), renamable and revocable; revoking closes the device's
  WebSocket (4401) and voids its signed URLs.
- "Require sign-in" (off by default, opt-in in Settings > Apps, or pinned
  by DOWNTIFY_REQUIRE_SIGN_IN): the web page then needs the password
  (scrypt, stdlib - no new dependency), which gives a 30-day sliding
  `downtify_session` cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure over HTTPS).
  Turning it on requires a password and signs the current browser in, so
  the page can't lock itself out. `python main.py auth-reset` is the way
  back in (clears password and sessions, keeps devices).
- Scopes: devices are "client" (library and media reads, /api/v1,
  search/previews, download requests, likes, Discover/listens, podcast
  playback and episode downloads, the WebSocket); everything else -
  settings, cookies, deleting files, upgrade/reconcile/archive, monitor
  and podcast subscription changes, artist edits, devices, pairing,
  password - needs a web session ("admin"). While sign-in isn't required
  everything stays open, but a request that *sends* a device token still
  has it checked (401 when revoked), so an app learns it was unpaired.
- One pure ASGI middleware enforces it for routes, both static mounts and
  the WebSocket, from a single rule table; anything under the protected
  prefixes that no rule names needs admin (deny by default), and a test
  walks every registered route and fails if one isn't classified on
  purpose.
- Signed URLs for headerless players (Chromecast): `exp`/`kid`/`sig` =
  HMAC-SHA256 over method, path and every other query parameter, key in
  /data/.auth_secret (0600), GET/HEAD only, TTL 60 s-24 h, void when the
  device is revoked or on "sign out everywhere" (key rotation). Issued by
  `POST /api/v1/sign` for audio and cover paths only. No long-lived token
  ever goes in a URL.
- WebSocket: device token on the handshake, the session cookie (with an
  Origin check against cross-site socket hijacking), or a single-use 60 s
  ticket (`POST /api/auth/ws-ticket`).
- Hardening: login/password/pairing attempts rate-limited per address
  (10 failures / 5 min, 429 + Retry-After); X-Forwarded-For/-Proto/-Host
  only believed from DOWNTIFY_TRUSTED_PROXIES; cookie-authenticated
  changes refused when Origin/Referer is another site. CORS no longer
  allows credentials: `allow_origins=['*']` with `allow_credentials=True`
  made Starlette reflect any origin, which would have let any website
  use a signed-in browser. The web app is same-origin and apps use a
  header, so nothing needs cross-origin cookies (an `npm run dev` on
  another port won't carry a session - irrelevant with sign-in off).
  Signed-URL signatures, tickets and codes are masked in request logs.
- All auth state lives in /data/downtify_auth.db and /data/.auth_secret,
  never in settings.json (which GET /api/settings hands out - that
  endpoint is admin-only once sign-in is required).

Server identity and API version (downtify/server_identity.py)
- `GET /api/server/info` (public): stable server id (/data/server.json),
  editable name (default: hostname; `PATCH /api/server`), version,
  `api_version: 1`, require_sign_in, capabilities (transcoding formats and
  bitrates, signed_urls, pairing, ...). The new mobile surface is
  versioned as `/api/v1/...` because the existing routes' shapes are
  coupled to the web app and must not change (CLAUDE.md).

Library sync (downtify/library_sync.py, sync_tracks in downtify_library.db)
- Stable track ids: same path -> same id (re-tags in place keep it); a
  new path takes a vanished track's id when exactly one vanished track
  has the same file name + size (move) or the same title/artist/album/
  length (rename); otherwise a new id. Moved *and* re-tagged in one sweep
  = new id + the old one deleted (documented).
- `GET /api/v1/library?since=<cursor>` change feed: one sequence number
  for every add/change/remove, removed ids kept 90 days, `full: true`
  (replace everything) for since=0, a too-old or unknown cursor. ETag/304.
  `refresh=true` forces a rescan. Rows add `artists` (the web app's split
  rule), `album_artist`, `album_id`/`artist_id` (the web app's exact
  grouping keys) and the audio format.
- The metadata cache now also stores codec, bitrate, sample rate and
  channels (META_VERSION 4, columns in both CREATE TABLE and
  _ADDED_COLUMNS); `GET /tracks` rows gain those fields (additive).
- `GET /api/v1/tracks/{id}` (+ `/lyrics`), `/api/v1/playlists` (track
  ids in order; listing logic moved from main.py to
  downtify/playlist_listing.py, same output), `GET|PUT /api/v1/likes` (by
  track id; `PUT /api/likes`'s body moved into `api.apply_like`).

Streaming and transcoding (downtify/transcode.py, mobile_routes.py)
- `GET|HEAD /api/v1/tracks/{id}/stream`: the original with full Range
  support and the registered audio types (audio/flac, not audio/x-flac),
  or `format=opus|aac|mp3&bitrate=96..320`.
- Transcode-to-cache-then-serve rather than piping ffmpeg: seeking (Range)
  and exact Content-Length must work, and a song transcodes in ~2 s
  (measured: 4-minute FLAC -> Opus 160 in 1.97 s cold, 6 ms cached). Cache
  in /data/transcode_cache keyed by source path/size/mtime + format +
  bitrate, LRU-bounded (DOWNTIFY_TRANSCODE_CACHE_MB, default 2 GB), at
  most DOWNTIFY_TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY (2) ffmpeg runs, identical requests
  share one run, and a run nobody waits for anymore (client disconnected)
  is killed and its partial file removed. A lossy original at or below
  the requested bitrate is served as is (`X-Downtify-Transcoded: no`).
- `GET|HEAD /api/v1/tracks/{id}/cover?size=150|300|600`: extracted once,
  scaled once with the image's ffmpeg (no Pillow), cached in
  /data/cover_thumbs, ETag/304.
- Offline downloads use the same endpoint (`download=true` adds
  Content-Disposition; resumable via Range).
- CORS exposes Accept-Ranges/Content-Length/Content-Range/ETag/

LAN discovery (downtify/discovery.py)
- mDNS/DNS-SD `_downtify._tcp` with TXT id/name/version/api/port/scheme/
  path, re-announced on rename, docker/bridge/veth interfaces skipped.

- WebSocket `library_changed` (debounced 2 s) whenever the library paths

  invalidation-listener hook in library_paths_cache - or when a sync finds

- All strings in the 8 locales; pure helpers in lib/auth.js with tests.

feat(library): replace a track's audio with a version picked by hand

When Downtify matches the wrong song or the wrong version (a live cut, a
remix, an upload with an intro), there was no way to fix it without
deleting the track - and losing its place in playlists. Now an admin
opens "Replace audio…" from a library track's menu, searches YouTube
Music and YouTube (or pastes a link to one video), picks the right
upload, and the file's audio is swapped for it.

What stays the same (downtify/audio_replace.py):
- The file: same path, same format (an .mp3 stays MP3 at the chosen
  bitrate, a .flac stays FLAC...), so M3Us, the playlist catalog, likes,
  Navidrome and the apps' track ids keep pointing at it.
- The tags: every tag of the old file (cover and embedded lyrics
  included) is copied onto the new audio as it is - ID3 in the version
  the file had, Vorbis comments and FLAC pictures, MP4 atoms. The .lrc
  sidecar is left alone.
- The date: the modification time is kept (no jump in "Recently added");
  the caches keyed on size notice the new file.
- Safety: the video is downloaded next to the file under the staging
  name the library scan already skips (<name>.downtify-upgrade.<ext>),
  checked to be readable audio, tagged, and only then moved over the
  old file. A failed download leaves the file untouched and its
  leftovers are removed.

API (admin): GET /api/library/replace/candidates (YouTube Music songs
first, then YouTube uploads, no repeats, each with its length and the
difference to the file's; a pasted link is that one video) and POST
/api/library/replace, which runs as a queue job with the usual progress
messages. song.replace = {file, video_id} marks it, so Retry in the
queue replaces again instead of downloading a new track, and a link
pasted there replaces with that video. Only mp3/flac/m4a/ogg/opus files.
The activity log records it (audio_replaced).

Downloader: the yt-dlp options, progress hook and download are split out
of _fetch_and_tag into _ydl_options, _progress_hook and a public
fetch_audio (target folder, name and format), which both use.

Web app: a "Replace audio" dialog (ReplaceAudioDialog, admins only) with
the track as it is, the search, the versions (thumbnail, source, length
and how far it is from the file's, an "open on YouTube" link) and the
job's progress; the library reloads when it's done. All 8 locales.

Fix: reading embedded lyrics from FLAC/Ogg/Opus files raised ValueError
(Vorbis comments refuse MP4's "©lyr" key), which /lyrics, the apps'
lyrics endpoint and the library upgrade scan hit; the lookup now skips
keys a format refuses.

Docs: new docs/features/replace-audio.md (in the nav), the two endpoints
in the API reference, library upgrade now points at it, features index,
users (admin-only), README; CLAUDE.md's library-upgrade note mentions
where audio replacement lives.

Tests: tests/test_audio_replace.py (formats, query, candidates and
links, replacing mp3/flac/m4a/opus/ogg keeps path, tags, lyrics, cover
and date, a failed download changes nothing, the HTTP routes and the
queue job, admins only), the Vorbis lyrics regression, and Vitest for
the dialog's helpers. Verified live: a real YouTube Music candidate
replaced a 5 s placeholder in Portishead/Dummy with the 304 s song at
320 kbps; path, tags, lyrics, date and the M3U were unchanged.
